questions.stem: Which molecule holds most of the nitrogen in the atmosphere?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Nitrates live in soil water, not in the air.
Ammonium compounds form after fixation, not in the open sky.
Proteins sit inside living tissues, not in the atmosphere.

questions.stem: What do nitrogen fixing bacteria change nitrogen gas into first?

options.explanation: No rock is made during fixation.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Nitrites appear later in nitrification, not in fixation.
Plants must build their own proteins from absorbed nitrates.

questions.stem: How do the bacteria inside root nodules relate to their leguminous host?

options.explanation: The bacteria actively fix nitrogen for the plant.
Nodule bacteria fix nitrogen; they are not there to decompose.

options.text: In a mutualistic relationship, fixing nitrogen for both partners
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The partnership feeds both sides; it is not parasitic.

questions.stem: After fixation, which ion do plant roots absorb to build proteins?

options.explanation: Plants take up nitrates; ammonium must be converted first.
Leaves cannot drink nitrogen gas; roots take nitrates.
Nitrites are an intermediate step, not the final uptake.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Two events beyond bacteria can fix nitrogen. Which pair fits?

options.text: Lightning strikes and the industrial production of fertilisers
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Rain does not split nitrogen gas.
These move water, not nitrogen.
They wear down rock but do not fix nitrogen gas.

questions.stem: State the role of nitrogen fixing bacteria.
questions.modelAnswer: Nitrogen fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds, which are then changed into nitrates in the soil.

questions.stem: Name the structures on leguminous plants that house nitrogen fixing bacteria.
questions.modelAnswer: Root nodules on leguminous plants such as peas, beans and clover house the nitrogen fixing bacteria.

questions.stem: Explain why plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly.
questions.modelAnswer: Plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly because nitrogen gas is inert, so it must first be fixed into ammonium compounds and then nitrates that roots can absorb.

questions.stem: A farmer sows clover among grass to improve the soil. Explain the benefit.
questions.modelAnswer: Clover is leguminous, so the nitrogen fixing bacteria in its root nodules add nitrates to the soil, enriching it for the grass.

questions.stem: How does a cow gain nitrogen for building its own proteins?

options.explanation: Stream water does not supply usable nitrogen this way.

options.text: By feeding on plants and digesting their proteins
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By absorbing nitrates through its skin
options.explanation: Cow skin cannot soak up soil ions; digestion does the work.
Animals cannot use nitrogen gas by breathing it.

questions.stem: A fox eats a rabbit. What happens to the nitrogen in the rabbit tissues?

options.text: It turns into nitrates inside the fox
options.explanation: Nitrification happens in soil, not inside animal bodies.

options.text: It stays locked in the rabbit forever
options.explanation: Feeding transfers the nitrogen; it does not stay put.

options.text: It transfers into the fox, which uses it to build animal proteins
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It leaves the fox immediately as gas
options.explanation: Nitrogen is built into tissue first, not vented as gas.

questions.stem: Which statement links plant proteins to animal proteins?

options.text: Animal proteins appear spontaneously without nitrogen
options.explanation: All proteins need nitrogen; none appears from nothing.

options.text: Plants convert animal proteins into nitrates
options.explanation: The flow runs from plant tissue into animals, not backwards.

options.text: Nitrogen skips digestion and jumps into muscle
options.explanation: Digestion is the step that unlocks the nitrogen.

options.text: Digested plant proteins supply nitrogen for building animal proteins
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Why can a top carnivore be described as a store of nitrogen?

options.text: Because nitrogen passed up every feeding step before reaching its body
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because it makes nitrogen from sunlight
options.explanation: No animal makes nitrogen from light.

options.text: Because its body traps air in fur
options.explanation: Fur does not store usable nitrogen.

options.text: Because it drinks more water than prey
options.explanation: Water intake is irrelevant to nitrogen storage.

questions.stem: In the chain grass, deer, lion, at which step does nitrogen first enter animal tissue?

options.text: At no point, animals store no nitrogen
options.explanation: Animal tissue is rich in protein, so it stores nitrogen.

options.text: At the deer, when it digests grass proteins
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Grass builds plant protein; animal tissue starts with the deer.

options.text: At the lion, straight from the air
options.explanation: The lion gains nitrogen by eating, not from air.

questions.stem: State how nitrogen reaches a carnivore in a food chain.
questions.modelAnswer: A carnivore gains nitrogen by feeding on other animals, digesting their proteins and using the nitrogen to build its own animal proteins.

questions.stem: Name the molecules that animals build using nitrogen from digested food.
questions.modelAnswer: Animals build animal proteins from the nitrogen obtained when they digest plant or prey tissue.

questions.stem: Explain why every organism in a food chain depends on nitrogen fixation somewhere upstream.
questions.modelAnswer: Every organism depends on nitrogen fixation because the chain starts with plants absorbing fixed nitrates, so without that first step no proteins could be built anywhere up the chain.

questions.stem: A herbicide wipes out most plants in a meadow. Predict the effect on nitrogen flow to the fox population.
questions.modelAnswer: With fewer plants, the herbivores lose their protein source and decline, so the foxes receive less nitrogen through their prey.

questions.stem: Which organisms return nitrogen from dead tissue to the soil as ammonia?

options.explanation: Denitrifiers send nitrogen back to the air; decomposers put it in the soil.
Nodule bacteria fix nitrogen, they do not release it from dead matter.

options.text: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia onward; the first release is by decomposers.

questions.stem: Put the steps of nitrification in the correct order.

options.explanation: That reverses the real sequence.

options.text: Ammonia, then nitrates, with no intermediate
options.explanation: Nitrites form between ammonia and nitrates.
Ammonia comes first, not after nitrites.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: In which soil conditions are denitrifying bacteria most active?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Airy soil is exactly where denitrifiers slow down.
Cold alone does not define denitrifier habitat; low oxygen does.

options.text: Soil rich in fresh fertiliser only
options.explanation: Nitrates are their substrate, but activity peaks without oxygen.

questions.stem: Why do farmers plough their fields?

options.explanation: Compaction favours denitrification; ploughing does the opposite.

options.text: Ploughing increases aeration, which reduces denitrification and preserves nitrates
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: To add nitrogen gas to the soil
options.explanation: Ploughing adds air, not nitrogen gas itself.
Farmers want fewer denitrifiers, since they destroy nitrates.

questions.stem: A marshy field loses its nitrate levels over a wet season. Which bacteria caused the loss?

options.explanation: Nitrifiers build nitrates, they do not destroy them.
Decomposers release ammonia; the nitrate loss points to denitrifiers.

options.text: Denitrifying bacteria converting nitrates back into nitrogen gas
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Fixers add nitrogen compounds; they do not strip nitrates.

questions.stem: State what nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into.
questions.modelAnswer: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrites and onwards into nitrates, which plants can absorb.

questions.stem: Name the process in which denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the atmosphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Denitrification is the process in which denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas.

questions.stem: Explain why waterlogged soil loses fertility faster than well-drained soil.
questions.modelAnswer: Waterlogged soil holds little oxygen, so denitrifying bacteria thrive there and convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, draining the soil of the nitrates plants need.

questions.stem: After a flood, a field stays waterlogged for weeks. Suggest one action and explain it.
questions.modelAnswer: Ploughing the field adds air to the soil, which suppresses the anaerobic denitrifying bacteria and protects the remaining nitrates.
